prompt_free_text:
This paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models built on top of foundation-model features. The central claim is that although recent CBM constructions can match strong feature-based baselines on the source domain, they can fail badly under deployment-time distribution shift, and that this can be remedied by adapting both the concept bank and the concept-to-label mapping using only unlabeled target data and no source samples. The proposed method, CONDA, combines three stages: concept-score alignment (CSA), linear probing adaptation (LPA), and a residual concept bottleneck (RCB) that adds new concepts at test time. Empirically, the paper reports substantial gains across several datasets and CBM construction methods, sometimes bringing concept-based performance close to or above non-interpretable baselines.

Overall, I find the paper interesting and timely. The problem is well motivated: interpretability methods are often evaluated only in-distribution, while deployment under shift is exactly where both reliability and explanations matter most. The paper also addresses a relatively underexplored intersection of topics: foundation models, concept bottlenecks, and source-free/test-time adaptation. The empirical results are promising, especially on Waterbirds and Metashift, where unadapted CBMs degrade sharply and CONDA recovers much of the lost performance. The paper is also commendably ambitious in trying to connect different failure modes to different adaptation modules.

That said, I have significant reservations about the conceptual framing, the strength of the methodological novelty, and several aspects of the empirical validation. My overall assessment is positive but cautious: the paper has clear merit and could be impactful, but it would benefit from sharper theoretical grounding, stronger baselines, and more careful treatment of what exactly is being adapted and what interpretability guarantees remain after adaptation.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation and empirical motivation. Figure 1 and Table 1 support the claim that CBMs are not automatically more robust than direct feature-based predictors under shift. This is an important corrective to a common intuition in interpretable ML. The paper also makes a useful distinction between low-level shifts, concept-level shifts, and incomplete concept sets, and uses this taxonomy to motivate different adaptation mechanisms. Even if the formalism is not fully rigorous in the causal sense, it is a helpful organizing principle for the method and experiments.

The empirical breadth is another strength. The method is tested across multiple datasets, multiple FM backbones, and multiple CBM construction approaches. The fact that CONDA improves three distinct CBM families is encouraging and suggests the approach is not narrowly overfit to one bottleneck construction. The gains on Waterbirds and Metashift are particularly notable, and the component analysis indicating that CSA helps more on low-level shifts while LPA/RCB help more on concept-level shifts is intuitively sensible.

However, the paper’s formal treatment of distribution shift and concept completeness is weaker than it first appears. The definitions in Section 2 are mathematically dressed up, but they do not yet yield actionable theory or guarantees. In particular, the distinction between “low-level shift” and “concept-level shift” is defined relative to a chosen concept mapping h and predictor g, not as an intrinsic property of the data-generating process. This makes the categories somewhat circular: a shift is “low-level” if the concept distribution does not change under the chosen concept extractor, and “concept-level” if the concept distribution changes but the prediction distribution should not. That may be acceptable as an operational taxonomy, but it should not be presented too strongly as a formal characterization of real-world shifts. Similarly, the completeness definition is existential and classifier-class dependent, but the paper does not derive tests, bounds, or diagnostics from it. As written, the formalism is more descriptive than theoretically substantive.

A related concern is that the method’s adaptation objectives rely on assumptions that are stronger than the paper emphasizes. CSA assumes access to source-domain class-conditional Gaussian statistics of concept scores, even though the source dataset itself is unavailable. This is a nontrivial form of source information. In many source-free adaptation settings, retaining such sufficient statistics may be acceptable, but the paper should be clearer that the method is not purely source-model-only. Moreover, the Gaussian assumption in concept space is convenient but not obviously justified, especially for concept scores derived from heterogeneous concept banks and high-dimensional FM embeddings. The paper would be stronger with evidence that these class-conditional distributions are approximately Gaussian, or at least that the method is robust to misspecification.

The pseudo-labeling setup also deserves more scrutiny. The method uses an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe FM predictions to pseudo-label target data, then adapts the CBM to match those pseudo-labels. This raises an important question: to what extent is CONDA simply distilling the non-interpretable FM classifier into the CBM at test time? If so, that may still be useful, but the framing should be more explicit. In particular, the claim that CONDA “aligns the CBM performance with that of non-interpretable classification” may partly reflect the fact that the pseudo-labels are generated by those non-interpretable predictors. This is not necessarily a flaw, but it changes the interpretation of the contribution. The method is less “discovering robust concepts from unlabeled target data” and more “using FM predictions to retune the concept bottleneck online.” A stronger discussion of this dependence would improve the paper.

This issue becomes especially important for interpretability. The paper argues that adapted concepts and residual concepts are better aligned with target data and more human-intuitive. But after LPA and especially RCB, the model is no longer constrained to preserve the original semantics of the source concept bank. CSA directly updates concept vectors in embedding space; RCB adds randomly initialized residual concepts optimized for predictive performance with only weak similarity/coherency regularization. It is therefore not obvious that the resulting bottleneck remains interpretable in the same sense as the original CBM. The paper provides qualitative examples on Waterbirds, which are encouraging, but this is not enough to support broad claims about interpretability preservation or improvement. At minimum, I would like to see quantitative evaluation of concept quality before and after adaptation, such as concept coherency, human naming consistency, retrieval purity, or overlap with known attributes where available. Otherwise, there is a risk that the method improves accuracy by drifting toward latent directions that are only post hoc nameable.

The residual concept bottleneck is an interesting idea, but its novelty relative to prior residual/incremental CBM work seems somewhat limited, especially given the cited Shang et al. 2024 paper on incremental residual CBMs. The main novelty here is applying such an idea in a test-time adaptation setting with unlabeled target data. That is still meaningful, but the paper should more carefully position what is genuinely new algorithmically versus what is a composition of existing ingredients: class-aware alignment, pseudo-label self-training, elastic-net linear adaptation, and residual concept expansion. As it stands, the method feels more like a well-engineered pipeline than a fundamentally new adaptation principle. That is acceptable for a systems-oriented contribution, but the paper occasionally overstates novelty.

The experimental section is promising but leaves several important questions unanswered. First, the baseline set is incomplete for the claimed problem. Since the paper positions itself as the first TTA method for CBMs, it should compare not only to unadapted CBMs but also to straightforward adaptations of existing TTA methods applied to the CBM pipeline. For example, adapting only the linear layer with entropy minimization or pseudo-label cross-entropy, adapting concept vectors with Tent-style objectives, or applying CAFA directly in concept space without the full CONDA pipeline. Some of these may be partially covered by ablations, but they should be explicit baselines in the main text. Otherwise it is hard to isolate the value of the proposed objectives from generic test-time fine-tuning.

Second, comparison to non-interpretable TTA baselines is also important. The paper compares against zero-shot and linear probing without adaptation, but if the claim is that CONDA closes the robustness gap while preserving interpretability, then the relevant question is how it compares to adapted non-interpretable models under the same unlabeled target data. If LP plus a standard TTA method still outperforms CONDA substantially, then the practical tradeoff looks different. Conversely, if CONDA matches adapted LP, that would be a much stronger result.

Third, some results in Table 1 are mixed in ways that deserve more discussion. On CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, CONDA improves some CBMs but degrades the Yeh et al. model. On Camelyon17, adaptation often hurts the strongest CBM. On Metashift, zero-shot is already very strong and some adapted CBMs still remain below it. These are not fatal issues, but the paper’s narrative is more uniformly positive than the table warrants. It would help to analyze when adaptation hurts and whether this correlates with pseudo-label quality, concept-bank quality, or mismatch between shift type and adaptation module.

Fourth, the evaluation protocol for online adaptation should be clarified carefully. Since the method adapts sequentially over test batches and predicts on the same batch used for adaptation, there is always a concern about transductive leakage or optimistic evaluation. This is common in online TTA, but the paper should state clearly whether predictions are measured before or after adaptation on each batch, and whether batch order is randomized once or multiple times. Reporting both online and episodic variants, or at least sensitivity to batch order and batch size, would strengthen confidence in the results.

There are also some technical details that need clarification or correction. The Mahalanobis distance formula in Section 3.1 appears to have a parenthesis typo. More importantly, covariance estimation and inversion in concept space can be unstable, especially when m is large relative to per-class sample counts. The paper should specify whether covariance matrices are diagonal, shrunk, or regularized, and how numerical stability is ensured. Similarly, the coherency regularizer in Eq. 13 is subtracted in the objective, meaning the method maximizes average similarity to top-k neighbors; this is reasonable, but the paper should explain why this promotes semantic coherence rather than simply collapsing concepts toward dense regions of feature space. The cosine similarity regularizer in Eq. 12 also seems to penalize raw cosine similarity rather than absolute similarity; if negative cosine values are allowed, the objective may encourage anti-alignment rather than orthogonality. Perhaps that is intended, but it should be discussed.

I also found the interpretability claims somewhat overstated relative to the evidence. The paper says CONDA “provides concept-based interpretations better tailored towards the test inputs,” but the evidence is mainly qualitative and localized to one dataset. Since adaptation changes the concept bank itself, there is a tension between stability and adaptability of explanations. Users may value explanations that remain semantically consistent across domains, not just ones that improve predictive fit. The paper should acknowledge this tradeoff more explicitly. In some applications, changing the meaning or importance of concepts at deployment may itself be undesirable unless carefully audited.

A further concern is fairness of the pseudo-labeling oracle. The pseudo-labels come from an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe predictors on the same FM backbone. This gives CONDA access to a strong auxiliary predictor that some CBM baselines may not have used during construction. If the goal is to adapt a deployed CBM, this may be realistic, but then the method depends on retaining not just the FM and CBM but also a source-trained LP head and zero-shot prompts. The deployment assumptions should be stated clearly. It would also be useful to report pseudo-label accuracy, confidence thresholds if any, and sensitivity to using only ZS, only LP, or self-labeling from the CBM.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real value. The central empirical observation is important, the problem is novel enough, and the proposed pipeline appears practically effective. My main recommendation is not to reject the direction, but to tighten the claims and strengthen the evidence. In particular, the paper would be substantially improved by: adding stronger TTA baselines for both CBMs and non-interpretable models; quantifying pseudo-label quality and its effect on adaptation; providing quantitative interpretability metrics before and after adaptation; clarifying the source-information assumptions for CSA; and discussing more candidly the cases where adaptation hurts or where the adapted CBM remains below simple FM baselines.

If accepted, I would encourage the authors to revise the presentation along the following lines. First, frame the theoretical section as a motivating taxonomy rather than a formal theory of shift. Second, be explicit that CONDA leverages FM-based pseudo-labels and source-domain concept statistics, and discuss the implications. Third, moderate claims about interpretability unless supported by quantitative evidence. Fourth, better position the novelty as test-time adaptation of CBMs via coordinated adaptation of concept space and label mapping, rather than implying each component is individually novel.

In summary, this is a thoughtful and potentially impactful paper on an important problem. Its main strengths are the relevance of the setting, the practical effectiveness of the method, and the empirical demonstration that CBMs are not inherently robust under shift. Its main weaknesses are limited theoretical depth, reliance on strong assumptions and auxiliary predictors, insufficiently rigorous interpretability evaluation, and missing adaptation baselines. I lean positive because the contribution is meaningful and likely to stimulate follow-up work, but I would want to see the above issues addressed for the paper to fully meet the standard of a top-tier conference.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model features under distribution shift. It argues that CBMs are not inherently robust after deployment, identifies three failure modes (non-robust concept bottleneck under low-level shift, non-robust classifier under concept-level shift, and incomplete concept sets), and proposes CONDA, a three-stage source-free adaptation framework using only unlabeled target data: concept-score alignment (CSA) to adapt concept vectors via pseudo-labeled Mahalanobis alignment to source class-conditional concept statistics, linear probing adaptation (LPA) to adapt the concept-to-label linear layer with elastic-net regularization, and a residual concept bottleneck (RCB) to add new target-specific concepts. Experiments across CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM construction methods show substantial target-domain gains over unadapted CBMs, sometimes approaching or exceeding non-interpretable baselines.
strengths: Addresses an interesting and timely problem at the intersection of interpretability, foundation models, and test-time adaptation; the problem setting is practically relevant.
The decomposition into three failure modes is intuitive and helps motivate the modular design of CSA, LPA, and RCB.
The method is reasonably general and can be combined with multiple CBM construction approaches and multiple FM backbones.
Empirical evaluation spans several datasets with different shift types and compares against multiple CBM baselines as well as zero-shot and linear-probe FM baselines.
Results show large improvements over unadapted CBMs on several target shifts, especially on Waterbirds and Metashift, suggesting the approach is practically useful.
The paper includes some interpretability analysis showing how concept reliance changes after adaptation and how residual concepts may capture missing semantics.
weaknesses: The theoretical framing of shift types and completeness is largely definitional and does not yield formal guarantees or testable criteria; several claims are more conceptual than rigorous.

The method relies heavily on pseudo-labels from zero-shot and linear-probe FM predictors, so gains may partly come from importing robustness from non-interpretable predictors rather than adapting the CBM itself.

The source-free setting is weakened by assuming access to class-conditional Gaussian statistics of source concept scores; this is effectively extra source information and its storage/privacy/feasibility implications are not fully discussed.

Empirical comparisons are incomplete in important places: there is little direct comparison to strong generic TTA baselines applied to the same CBM or to the underlying linear probe, making it hard to isolate the novelty advantage.

Some results are inconsistent or negative: adaptation hurts strong CBMs on CIFAR100 and Camelyon17 in several cases, and even under low-level shift CSA/LPA/RCB combined can underperform simpler variants; these failure cases are not deeply analyzed.
Interpretability claims are suggestive but not quantitatively validated; there is no rigorous metric showing that adapted or residual concepts are more faithful, stable, or human-meaningful.
The online adaptation protocol may be sensitive to batch order and error accumulation from pseudo-labels, but robustness to these factors is not clearly established.
methodological_flaws: The formal definition of low-level shift as preserving the concept-score distribution (Eq. 2) is too strong and effectively bakes robustness into the definition; many realistic corruptions alter concept scores even if semantics are unchanged. This weakens the scientific usefulness of the taxonomy.

Definition 1 of concept completeness is problematic: equality of prediction distributions across domains does not imply semantic sufficiency of the concept set, nor does it ensure correct labels. Matching marginal prediction distributions is much weaker than preserving conditional label relationships.

The CSA objective assumes class-conditional Gaussianity of concept scores and uses Mahalanobis distances based on stored source means/covariances, but there is no empirical validation that this assumption holds for CBM concept scores across datasets or that covariance estimates are well-conditioned, especially in high dimensions.

Pseudo-labels are produced by an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe predictors trained/accessed outside the CBM. This introduces a strong auxiliary supervision signal that may dominate adaptation. The paper does not disentangle how much improvement comes from pseudo-label quality versus the proposed adaptation objectives.

The source-free claim is somewhat overstated because adaptation requires source-derived class-conditional statistics and a source-trained linear probe for pseudo-labeling. This is not equivalent to having only the source model.

The residual concept branch improves accuracy but may undermine interpretability: randomly initialized residual vectors optimized only through pseudo-label cross-entropy plus weak regularizers can become arbitrary discriminative directions rather than coherent concepts. The paper provides anecdotal examples but no systematic validation.

The empirical evidence does not consistently support the full method: on CIFAR100 and Camelyon17, CONDA often degrades the strongest CBM baseline (Yeh et al.), indicating that the method may not be reliably beneficial and that conclusions about broad effectiveness should be tempered.

There appears to be a notation/reference inconsistency: the text in LPA refers to predictions of the target-domain CBM via Eqn. (3), but the target-domain CBM is defined in Eq. (5). Such inconsistencies are minor editorially but reduce confidence in mathematical precision.
